citations.quote: The essential contribution of this paper is the requirement elicitation and specification of system-wide qualities such as availability, performance, and security using quality attribute scenarios. The effect of using the quality-based scenarios is that it allows more rigorous treatment of non-functional requirements and hence proper selection of an architecture modeling to satisfy these requirements.

In particular, this paper discusses the application of the model-based requirements engineering (MBRE) method to the development of the CubeSat cyber-physical system currently under development at the University of North Dakota (UND) [7].

The project is a student-run effort [14, 15] that aims to reduce the parts cost required for building a small spacecraft to below $5,000 [16]. To do this, the project is using open source software and open hardware concepts that will allow other developers to use the software and hardware designs at no cost to them.

The operating software is responsible for ensuring that the satellite is always operating within the parameters defined and that it performs the tasks assigned by the operators. This all has to be done as efficiently as possible to minimize power consumption and maximize task completion levels.
The payload software will run on separate processing units and these will only be powered on when they are needed, to conserve the limited spacecraft battery.

Onboard image processing will serve several purposes. First, because of the limited bandwidth between the spacecraft and the ground station, an approach to reduce data needed to be transmitted is required. Second, it is desirable to produce ready-for-user data products that could be downloaded directly from the satellite by a prospective user.

The CubeSat's operational capabilities have been defined using UML scenarios and use cases. This work reports on the practicality of quality-attribute (QA) scenarios (based on the approach presented in [17]) to document nonfunctional requirements (NFR) of CubeSats, which is considered to be the prerequisite for evaluation and further investigation.

The rational for using quality-attributes scenarios are to serve two objectives of the CubeSat project: 1) to specify quality attribute requirements by incorporating a level of detail in the form of templates to resolve the ambiguity normally attributed with existing approaches (e.g., natural language), and 2) to validate the suitability of architectural design decisions using tradeoff analysis to ensure that the architecture meets the quality attribute requirements.
To meet the first objective, sixteen quality attribute scenarios were generated to specify key quality attributes
To meet the second objective, these scenarios will be used for architecting a future CubeSat system such that the selected architecture optimizes its key quality attributes (NFRs).

The selected software architecture (ATAM [17]) then will be precisely defined using the model-based engineering language AADL [17, 36, 37] and analyzed using OSATE [8] to ensure that the software architecture supports the specified qualities.

The first step in this process is to capture system requirements for the CubeSat using quality attributed scenarios [17] and UML use case scenarios. To this end, two templates were used to specify both functional and nonfunctional requirements. Extended version of use-case scenarios that incorporated references to non-functional or functional requirements were used to establish proper treatability among requirements. Quality attribute scenarios and templates developed by Bass, et al. at Carnegie Mellon University [17] were used to document the nonfunctional requirements of the CubeSat.

Figure 1 depicts the system architecture of the CubeSat system. The architecture consists of three main sub-systems: the off-board system (ground station and communications), the onboard or cyber-system (image and data processors), physical systems (camera and actuator).
The CubeSat mission will have a relatively short duration of roughly three months (based on the currently projected orbit).

All formal software requirements must satisfy (at least) two critical properties: specificity and verifiability. Therefore, every single software requirement must be written in a precise, quantifiable and testable way to minimize subjectivity.

citations.quote: The CubeSat system battery is a prime example of such a physical system. If the battery loses charge, the system will shut-down and be nonoperational. To circumvent this issue, the charge capacity of the battery is constantly monitored and the system is placed in a low-energy state if the battery drops to critical levels.
Battery should never fall below 10% charge

citations.quote: Development of CubeSats is still ongoing at University of North Dakota. The research presented in this paper is a critical step in furthering the analysis, design, development, and testing of a CPS such as the CubeSat using a modern software engineering approach.
An important part of the system requirements is quality attributes that can be used to test the suitability of the design related to the requirements.

One of the key shortcomings of QAs' approach is the way QAs are structured using the utility tree [17] approach. Utility trees use an ad-hoc decomposition technique. This, in turn, results in obscuring the other quality attributes (that have commonalities).

Another issue related to scenario generation using the QAs approach is that it works only with a handful of QAs with well-established quality models. The approach does not scale up to create QA's scenarios for new quality attributes such as greenability or sustainability, which currently do not have standard quality models to characterize them.

Finally, the practicality of these models to generate scenarios is an open question. For example, for the CubeSat project, students had difficulties generating scenarios for even quality attributes (such as performance) with well-established quality models. In general, to generate various scenarios for different QAs, the developer must possess an extensive background in and understanding of these qualities and their impact on one another.

Future work will rank and prioritize scenarios generated during this work to perform the trade-off analysis procedure outlined in ATAM to select the optimal architecture that best meet the CubeSat's NFRs.

The selected architectureal style (or domain specific architecture) will be specified using the Architecture Analysis and Design Language (AADL) in order to describe and analyze the non-functionalities of the CubeSat. To this end, we plan to divert the output generated by the AADL parser to an appropriate analysis tool supported by OSATE to evaluate the results.
A subset of the work presented herein was presented at the Research Experience for Undergraduates Poster Session at the 2015 AIAA/USU Conference on Small Satellites.
